findings.issue_text: [High/concurrency] Legacy writes run as independent goroutines without ordering, allowing rapid create/update/delete operations to reach legacy storage out of order and leave stale or recreated data.

[High/data] Asynchronous writes derive their timeout context from the HTTP request context, so request completion can cancel slow legacy writes before the intended 10-second timeout and break dual-write consistency.

[High/data] Update passes the original UpdatedObjectInfo to legacy storage instead of the object returned by unified storage, potentially producing different content or failing resource-version and precondition checks.
[Medium/data] Delete returns immediately when unified storage reports NotFound, leaving any stale legacy copy undeleted.

[Medium/performance] Successful delete latency uses the object name as a metrics label instead of options.Kind, creating unbounded label cardinality and potentially increasing Prometheus memory usage.

[Medium/test_gap] Tests neither wait for asynchronous legacy operations nor call AssertExpectations, so they can pass when legacy create/update/delete operations never execute or finish after the test.
[Low/bug] Unified-storage failures in Create and Update are recorded with recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, attributing primary-store failures and latency to the wrong backend.
[Low/bug] Asynchronous legacy DeleteCollection records duration with recordStorageDuration instead of the legacy recorder, corrupting per-backend latency and error metrics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [High/concurrency] Legacy writes run as independent goroutines without ordering, allowing rapid create/update/delete operations to reach legacy storage out of order and leave stale or recreated data.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in DualWriterMode3, legacy storage operations (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) are now executed in separate goroutines with `go func()`. These goroutines run independently without any synchronization or ordering guarantees. If a client rapidly performs create->update->delete operations, the legacy storage could receive these out of order (e.g., delete before create completes, or update before create). This could leave legacy storage in an inconsistent state with stale or incorrectly recreated data. The code explicitly shows `go func()` blocks for legacy operations in Create (line 47), Delete (line 87), Update (line 109), and DeleteCollection (line 131), all without any coordination mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [High/data] Asynchronous writes derive their timeout context from the HTTP request context, so request completion can cancel slow legacy writes before the intended 10-second timeout and break dual-write consistency.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection methods, goroutines are spawned that use `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)` where `ctx` is derived from the HTTP request context. When the HTTP request completes (after the Storage operation succeeds), the parent context gets cancelled, which will immediately cancel the derived timeout context in the goroutine, potentially before the 10-second timeout and before the Legacy operation completes. This breaks dual-write consistency as legacy writes may be cancelled prematurely. The correct approach would be to use `context.Background()` or `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent for the timeout context in the goroutines.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [High/data] Update passes the original UpdatedObjectInfo to legacy storage instead of the object returned by unified storage, potentially producing different content or failing resource-version and precondition checks.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that Update passes the original UpdatedObjectInfo to legacy storage instead of the object returned by unified storage. Looking at the diff, the new Mode3 Update implementation runs the legacy update in a goroutine with the same objInfo parameter. However, this is actually the intended behavior for Mode3 - it's a fire-and-forget async write to legacy storage. The old code was more complex, fetching the object first and wrapping it, but the new simplified approach is consistent with the other Mode3 methods (Create, Delete, DeleteCollection) which all use goroutines for legacy writes. The finding mischaracterizes this as a bug when it's actually a deliberate simplification of the async legacy write pattern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Medium/data] Delete returns immediately when unified storage reports NotFound, leaving any stale legacy copy undeleted.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that Delete returns immediately when unified storage reports NotFound, leaving legacy copies undeleted. However, looking at the diff for Mode3's Delete method, the new implementation does NOT have special NotFound handling - it simply returns on ANY error from Storage.Delete. The old code (being removed) had NotFound handling with apierrors.IsNotFound, but the new code removes this. More importantly, the new code runs Legacy.Delete in a goroutine regardless of the Storage result - if Storage.Delete succeeds, the goroutine will attempt to delete from Legacy. The finding misreads the diff - the new code actually removes the NotFound special case, and legacy deletion happens asynchronously after successful storage deletion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Medium/test_gap] Tests neither wait for asynchronous legacy operations nor call AssertExpectations, so they can pass when legacy create/update/delete operations never execute or finish after the test.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the Mode3 tests don't wait for the goroutines spawned by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection operations. Looking at the diff, the implementation uses `go func()` to run legacy operations asynchronously (e.g., in Create: `go func() { ... d.Legacy.Create(...) }`), but the tests don't have any synchronization mechanism to wait for these goroutines. The tests also don't call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` to verify all expected mock calls were made. However, this is somewhat mitigated because the tests primarily verify the Storage operations (which are synchronous) and the legacy operations are intentionally fire-and-forget in Mode3. Still, this is a legitimate test gap for newly added async behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Low/bug] Unified-storage failures in Create and Update are recorded with recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, attributing primary-store failures and latency to the wrong backend.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for dualwriter_mode3.go, in the Create method at line 42, when storage creation fails, it calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` - this is incorrect because it should be `recordStorageDuration` since the failure is in Storage, not Legacy. Similarly, in the Update method at line 103, when storage update fails, it calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. This is a real bug where storage failures are being attributed to the legacy backend in metrics.
